rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - two-year field experiment (2008, 2009) at Sarabuim, Egypt, randomized block factorial design with surface vs subsurface drip x four irrigation levels (100/80/60/40% ETc), three replicates. Q2: Yield and Yield Components / Table 2 - drip system and irrigation level had significant effects on tuber yield; reducing water to 80% ETc under subsurface drip gave yield comparable to surface drip at full supply, so 20% of irrigation water can be saved without affecting potato yield; SSD averaged 36.32 vs 30.18 t/ha for SD. Q4: Soil Water Distribution / Fig. 1 - gravimetric soil moisture sampled below the dripper at depths to 70 cm and radial distances to 35 cm at each growth stage; subsurface drip kept >16% water content to 40 cm where potato roots were confined, which the authors link to the higher yield. Q7: Yield and Yield Components - authors state that higher yield can be achieved by placing the drip line sufficiently below the soil surface so water reaches the most active root zone and evaporation losses are cut; conclusion restricted to drip-irrigated potato on sandy soil texture.
rows.notes: The passage misstates the study: this paper is on potato (cv. Cara), not tomato, and irrigation levels are percentages of crop evapotranspiration (ETc), not of field capacity. The review may have conflated it with the other Badr et al. (2010) paper on tomato fertigation listed in the reference list. The technology (drip) and the effect (high yield with reduced water at 80% supply) are nonetheless reported here as own results, so Q2 is rated yes with this caveat. Yield measured by one method only (10 plants per subplot). One site, one soil, one crop. Table 2 gives LSD values only, no SD/SE/CI; the 'data not shown' remark for stressed treatments is not a stated limitation.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own two-year field experiment with surface and subsurface drip at four ETc levels on sandy soil. Q2: Water and Fertilizer Use Efficiency / Table 3 and Abstract - subsurface drip recorded higher WUE than surface drip at all irrigation levels (e.g. 212-215 vs 138-155 kg/ha/mm at 40% ETc); 80% ETc under SSD matched full-supply SD yield, indicating a 20% water saving. Q4: Soil Water Distribution / Fig. 1 - measured soil moisture profiles show the surface stayed dry (about 12%) under SSD while adequate water remained in the root zone and was not lost to deep percolation, the mechanism the authors give for reduced evaporation and higher WUE. Q7: Yield and Yield Components and Conclusions - the water saving is tied to placing the drip line sufficiently below the surface and to sandy soil conditions; subsurface line was buried at the shallowest depth consistent with low capillary forces of sandy soil.
rows.notes: Same passage misstatement as the previous row: crop is potato not tomato, and treatments are % ETc, not % field capacity. Water use was applied (not measured) per treatment, with WUE computed as yield/applied water; soil evaporation was not measured directly, only inferred from soil moisture distribution. No second independent method, single site, no stated limitations, no dispersion measures for WUE in Table 3.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own field experiment, 2008-2009, SD vs SSD x four irrigation levels, potato on sandy soil in Egypt. Q2: Water and Fertilizer Use Efficiency / Table 3 - at all irrigation levels SSD recorded higher WUE than SD, maximum at 40% ETc; Soil Water Distribution - under SSD a great deal of soil water remained in the root zone and was not lost to deep percolation. Q4: Fig. 1 and Soil Water Distribution - gravimetric soil moisture mapped by depth and distance from the dripper at each growth stage, showing the dry surface and water retention in the 0-40 cm root zone under SSD, which the authors use to explain the reduced evaporation and higher WUE. Q7: Yield and Yield Components / Conclusions - effect attributed to drip line placement sufficiently below the surface and stated for sandy soil texture; wetting pattern depends on predominance of gravity over capillary forces in sandy soil.
rows.notes: The study supports the WP (WUE) part of the passage and gives observational evidence (soil moisture profiles) on reduced deep percolation; soil evaporation was not measured, only inferred. The context sentence (effects vary with management, climate, soil) is not something this single-site study can show. WUE based on applied water, one method. No limitations stated beyond 'data not shown'. Table 3 reports WUE without SD/SE/CI; LSD in Table 2 is not a dispersion measure.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own two-year field experiment comparing surface and subsurface drip under four irrigation levels.
rows.notes: The study does not measure weed growth or any pest-control outcome. It reports only that the soil surface remained relatively dry under subsurface drip at all growth stages (Soil Water Distribution, Fig. 1), which is a precondition for reduced weed growth; the weed-control benefit of SSD is mentioned only in the Introduction as a result from other work (Enciso et al. 2005; Lamm and Camp 2007; Selim et al. 2009). Hence upstream only.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a two-year, single-site potato trial on sandy soil in Egypt comparing surface and subsurface drip at 100/80/60/40% ETc. Review LIT_0038 appears to have confused this paper with the other Badr et al. (2010) tomato fertigation paper (Healthy Plants 62(1):11-19) cited in its reference list; the passage's 'tomato' and '80% of field capacity' are not in this study.
